claims.text: Damaged 316L stainless steel with microstructural degradation and surface defects is predisposed to hot cracking during conventional fusion welding.
CoCrFeNiMo0.85 can be deposited by laser metal deposition or laser cladding onto a 316L stainless-steel substrate.
Adding preheating or a thin buffer layer before cladding enhances interfacial bonding.
Adding preheating or a thin buffer layer mitigates residual-stress development.
Controlled laser power and scanning speed, inert processing, and preheating or a buffer layer will minimize dilution and reduce the heat-affected zone.
The modified process will form a dense, ultrafine-grained, homogeneous CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating.
The buffer layer will produce robust interfacial bonding in the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating on 316L.
The buffer layer will minimize segregation and residual thermal gradients.
Rapid localized melting and rapid solidification refine the coating microstructure.
A fine-grained fusion-zone structure can reduce elemental microsegregation.
Laser cladding avoids formation of the large fusion zone associated with traditional fusion-welding repair.
Reduced thermal mismatch and residual stress from preheating or a buffer layer will prevent hot cracking.
CoCrFeNiMo0.85 deposited on stainless steel is less prone to manufacturing cracking than the same coating deposited on carbon steel.
The modified coating will significantly increase microhardness relative to fusion-weld repair and an untreated surface.
The modified coating will improve corrosion and erosion resistance relative to fusion-weld repair and an untreated surface.
The modified coating will reduce hot-cracking susceptibility relative to fusion-weld repair and an untreated surface.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs typically exhibit large thermal gradients and hot cracking.
The method is expected to be effective for localized repair of 316L components only when the laser, preheating, and buffer-layer parameters are appropriately calibrated.
